title: CSV Coordinate Deduplicator: Count the Repeats
description: Audit a coordinate CSV for repeated points with the CSV Coordinate Deduplicator — valid pairs, unique count and repeat count. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a six-row city file with Denver pasted twice reports 5 unique pairs and 1 repeat — the row that would have drawn two pins on the same spot and voted twice in every average.
quick_answer: The CSV Coordinate Deduplicator audits a coordinate list for repeated map points before the file reaches a map, a routing workflow or a spatial database. Paste the CSV and read the verdict: how many valid pairs exist, how many are unique, and how many repeat a pair.
steps_intro: Duplicates hide in plain sight. Count them before they cost you:

body.t: Merged exports breed repeats. Dedupe the audit here, clean in your editor, and import once — the
Two pins on one spot look like one pin and count like two in every statistic. The deduplicator tells you how much of your map is echo.
A join that doubles rows doubles coordinates. When the row count smells wrong, the repeat count here isolates the geometry side of the bug.
Field devices re-upload; sync tools hiccup. A repeat census after each collection round keeps the master file honest.
Six rows, five cities, Denver twice: unique 5, repeats 1. Nothing about the rows looks wrong individually — deduplication is a whole-file property, which is why eyeballing never finds it.

40.7128 and 40.71280 are the same number; 40.7128 and 40.7129 (11 metres apart) are different pairs and both count as unique. Exact-pair matching is the rule — rounding games belong to deliberate cleaning, discussed in the FAQs.

popular_table.note: Matching is on the exact coordinate pair. Trailing-zero dress (40.71280) parses to the same number and matches; genuinely different coordinates never merge by accident.

faq: It audits and reports — the deleting is yours, in your editor, with the counts as your checklist. Tools that silently delete rows teach users not to trust tools.
What about rows that differ only in name?
Same coordinates, different labels still repeat as points. Whether they are one place with two names or two tenants of one building is your knowledge, not the pair’s.
A row without valid coordinates is not a pair at all — the validator’s census covers it. This tool counts within the valid universe.
Coordinates are numbers; ‘40.7128’ and ‘ 40.7128 ’ parse alike. Text-column quirks do not reach the pair comparison.

Rounding coordinates to 4–5 decimals first (the Coordinate Rounding Tool) merges jitter-twins from GPS re-reads — a legitimate cleaning strategy when the jitter is noise, a data crime when it is signal.
Deliveries, visits and events repeat at addresses by nature. If repeats are frequency, keep them and let them weigh — dedupe is for accidents.
The first occurrence is the original; later ones are the repeats. The count is order-blind, the labels are not.
